title: View of the Villa Lante on the Janiculum in Rome
medium: Brush and watercolor over traces of graphite

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1967

altText: A watercolor view of a villa and its surroundings on a hill in Rome, painted in soft, hazy blues, greens, and warm tones with delicate brushwork.

context: A watercolor by John Robert Cozens (1752–1797), an English landscape artist, dated 1782–83 in the Met's record. The title places the view at the Villa Lante on the Janiculum, a hill in Rome. The medium is brush and watercolor over traces of graphite.

descriptions.k: A villa and the land around it, on a hill in Rome, Italy. The paint is soft and misty. The artist used a brush with lots of water. What do you think you could see from up here?
descriptions.g12: John Robert Cozens painted this view of a villa on a hill in Rome, Italy. He used watercolor with soft, gentle colors. The air looks hazy, as if it is a quiet, warm day. What would it feel like to stand there and look out?
descriptions.g35: John Robert Cozens was an English artist who traveled to Italy and painted its landscapes. This watercolor, made in 1782 or 1783, shows the Villa Lante, a house on the Janiculum hill in Rome. Look at how the colors fade softly into the distance. How does he make the air look hazy and the view feel wide?
descriptions.g68: Cozens painted this view in 1782 to 1783, when he was in Italy. Instead of detailed outlines, he used brush and layers of watercolor to build soft hills, buildings, and sky. Notice how distant parts become paler and bluer, a method artists call atmospheric perspective. Why might a painter care more about mood and light than about every brick, and how can a landscape feel like a memory?
descriptions.g910: In View of the Villa Lante on the Janiculum in Rome, Cozens uses translucent watercolor over faint graphite to build a broad, atmospheric landscape. Layers of wash create recession, and the villa becomes part of a larger view rather than a portrait of a building. His work is often discussed as influential for later British landscape painters. Consider how the sheet balances topographical identification with a poetic sense of distance and light.
descriptions.g1112: Cozens's Roman view of 1782–83 exemplifies the late eighteenth-century turn in British watercolor toward landscape as a field of atmosphere and feeling, achieved through layered washes over minimal drawing. The title identifies a specific site, yet the sheet foregrounds light, haze, and spatial depth. Cozens is often cited as an influence on later landscape painters, but the record for this sheet gives only title, date, medium, and tags. Consider how a travel view negotiates record, taste for the picturesque, and individual sensibility.

teacherNote.context: John Robert Cozens (1752–1797) was an English landscape watercolorist who worked in Italy in the early 1780s. This sheet shows a view at the Villa Lante on the Janiculum hill in Rome.
directions: Have students paint a three-layer landscape, near, middle, and far, making each layer paler and bluer.
Ask students to find where the picture shows the most and the least detail and explain why.
Discuss why travelers brought home pictures of places they visited and how people do that today.
